title: Naming the Exception: A Menos Que, A No Ser Que, Salvo Que

sections.title: The one thing that would change it
sections.content: You know *a menos que* "unless" from B1 Unit 21. This lesson adds two phrases with the same meaning, *a no ser que* and *salvo que* (*salvo que* is slightly more written). They name the only circumstance that would stop the main clause from holding, so the main clause says what happens if that exception does not occur: *Iremos al parque a menos que llueva* means "we will go, unless it rains". All three are followed by the subjunctive, because the exception has not happened yet. After a present or future main verb use the present subjunctive; after a conditional or past main verb use the imperfect subjunctive.

sections.title: Three ways to say "unless"
rows: except if (the same idea, built like si)

items.spanish: Iremos al parque a menos que llueva.
items.english: We will go to the park unless it rains.

items.spanish: No saldremos a no ser que mejore el tiempo.
items.english: We will not go out unless the weather improves.

items.spanish: Nadie puede entrar al archivo salvo que tenga permiso.
items.english: No one can enter the archive unless they have permission.

items.spanish: Dijo que vendría a menos que tuviera trabajo.
items.english: She said she would come unless she had work.

items.spanish: Salgo temprano, salvo si hay mucho trabajo.
items.english: I leave early, except if there is a lot of work.

sections.content: Never use the indicative after *a menos que*, *a no ser que* or *salvo que*: *a menos que llueva*, not *a menos que llueve*. Only *salvo si* works like the *si* you already know, with the indicative.
